# The short answer {.unnumbered}

## What this note assumes

In the full learning path, read
[Measure and probability foundations](measure-probability-foundations.qmd),
[Lebesgue measure and absolute continuity](lebesgue-measure-integration-and-densities.qmd),
and [the Bayesian measure-notation guide](../Bayesian/bayes-measure-d-concept.qmd)
first. The core Dirac definition needs only the first two. No knowledge of
generalized functions or functional analysis is assumed; the physics notation
is translated below.

The **Dirac measure** at a point $a$ is the probability measure

$$
\delta_a(A)=
\begin{cases}
1,&a\in A,\\
0,&a\notin A.
\end{cases}
$$

It puts all probability at $a$.

The **Dirac delta function** $\delta(x-a)$ is not an ordinary real-valued
function. It is a generalized function, or distribution, used to express the
same point-evaluation operation in calculus and physics notation.

In probability and Bayesian nonparametrics, the measure notation
$\delta_a(dx)$ is usually the safest notation.

# The Dirac probability measure {#the-dirac-probability-measure}

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathscr X)$ be a measurable space and let $a\in\mathcal X$.
Define

$$
\delta_a:\mathscr X\to[0,1],
\qquad
\delta_a(A)=\mathbf 1(a\in A).
$$

It is a probability measure because

- $\delta_a(\emptyset)=0$;
- $\delta_a(\mathcal X)=1$;
- for pairwise disjoint $A_1,A_2,\ldots$, the point $a$ belongs to at most one
  set, so countable additivity holds.

Names used for the same object include

- Dirac measure at $a$;
- unit point mass at $a$;
- degenerate distribution concentrated at $a$.

# Its defining integration property {#dirac-integration-property}

For every measurable integrable function $h$,

$$
\boxed{
\int_{\mathcal X}h(x)\delta_a(dx)=h(a)
}.
\tag{1}
$$

This follows first for indicator functions:

$$
\int \mathbf 1_A(x)\delta_a(dx)
=\delta_a(A)
=\mathbf 1_A(a),
$$

and then extends to simple functions and general integrable functions.

“Measurable” means the function is compatible with the sigma-fields, so its
level-set events are measurable. “Integrable” means the integral of its
absolute value is finite. A **simple function** takes only finitely many
values and can be written as a finite sum of weighted indicators. These terms
are developed in the [measure-integration note](lebesgue-measure-integration-and-densities.qmd#integration-with-respect-to-a-measure).

Equation (1) says that integration against $\delta_a$ evaluates the integrand
at $a$.

# Discrete distributions are sums of Dirac measures {#dirac-discrete-laws}

If $X$ takes values $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ with probabilities $p_1,p_2,\ldots$, its
distribution can be written

$$
P_X=\sum_jp_j\delta_{x_j}.
$$

For any measurable $A$,

$$
P_X(A)=\sum_jp_j\delta_{x_j}(A)
=\sum_jp_j\mathbf 1(x_j\in A),
$$

and for any integrable $h$,

$$
\int h(x)P_X(dx)=\sum_jp_jh(x_j).
$$

This is the usual discrete expectation written as a measure integral.

# Why a Dirac measure has no ordinary Lebesgue density {#dirac-not-lebesgue-density}

Let $\lambda$ be Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$. If $\delta_a$ had a density
$q=d\delta_a/d\lambda$, then $\delta_a$ would be absolutely continuous with
respect to $\lambda$:

$$
\lambda(A)=0\implies\delta_a(A)=0.
$$

But

$$
\lambda(\{a\})=0
\quad\text{while}\quad
\delta_a(\{a\})=1.
$$

Therefore

$$
\delta_a\not\ll\lambda
$$

and no ordinary Lebesgue density $d\delta_a/d\lambda$ exists. The Dirac measure
is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure.

In this example, **singular** means that all of $\delta_a$'s mass is
concentrated on the set $\{a\}$, which has Lebesgue measure zero.

This is why no ordinary function can simultaneously be zero away from $a$,
have a finite or infinite value only at $a$, and integrate to one under
Lebesgue integration. A value at one Lebesgue-null point contributes zero to an
ordinary integral.

# What the “Dirac delta function” means {#dirac-delta-generalized-function}

This section is optional for reading Walker. It is included so that physics
and engineering notation will not be confused with an ordinary PDF.

In generalized-function theory, $\delta_a$ acts on a sufficiently smooth test
function $\varphi$ by

$$
\langle\delta_a,\varphi\rangle=\varphi(a).
$$

Physics notation often writes this as

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
\varphi(x)\delta(x-a)\,dx
=\varphi(a).
\tag{2}
$$

Equation (2) is valid when interpreted as the action of a generalized function
or, equivalently here, as integration with respect to the Dirac measure. It
does not make $\delta(x-a)$ an ordinary probability density.

A **test function** is simply a well-behaved input function—usually smooth and
zero outside a bounded region—against which a generalized function is
evaluated. A generalized function is defined through what it does to all such
inputs, rather than through a finite value at every point. For probability
work, the measure identity (1) is sufficient; no generalized-function theory
is required.

The informal picture of an infinitely tall, zero-width spike with area one can
aid memory, but it is not a definition.

# Notation guide

| Notation | Recommended interpretation |
|---|---|
| $\delta_a$ | Dirac probability measure at $a$ |
| $\delta_a(A)$ | $1$ if $a\in A$, otherwise $0$ |
| $\delta_a(dx)$ | Integrate with respect to the Dirac measure |
| $\delta_a(x)$ | Context-dependent shorthand; avoid if it suggests an ordinary function |
| $\delta(x-a)$ | Generalized-function notation common in physics |

In probability notes, write

$$
F(dx)=\sum_jp_j\delta_{x_j}(dx)
$$

rather than calling
$\sum_jp_j\delta_{x_j}(x)$ an ordinary density.

# Bayesian bootstrap {#dirac-bayesian-bootstrap}

Given observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, a Bayesian-bootstrap draw is the random
probability measure

$$
F^{(b)}=\sum_{i=1}^nW_i^{(b)}\delta_{X_i},
\qquad
(W_1^{(b)},\ldots,W_n^{(b)})
\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,\ldots,1).
\tag{3}
$$

For a function $h$,

$$
\int h(x)F^{(b)}(dx)
=\sum_{i=1}^nW_i^{(b)}h(X_i).
$$

If some observed values are equal, (3) may list the same Dirac measure more
than once. Combining equal locations gives the same $F^{(b)}$ with their
weights added.

Because $E(W_i)=1/n$, the posterior mean measure is the empirical distribution:

$$
E\{F^{(b)}(A)\mid X_{1:n}\}
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1(X_i\in A).
$$

This object has atoms at the observed values. It is not a Lebesgue density.

An **atom** is a point receiving positive probability. Here $X_i$ is an atom
whenever its combined random weight is positive.

# Dirichlet-process draws and mixtures {#dirac-dp-draws-mixtures}

A stick-breaking representation of a Dirichlet-process draw has the form

$$
G=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}W_j\delta_{\Theta_j}.
$$

The random measure $G$ is discrete. If it is used as a mixing measure with a
continuous kernel $k$, however,

$$
f_G(x)=\int k(x\mid\theta)G(d\theta)
=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}W_jk(x\mid\Theta_j)
$$

can be a smooth density. The Dirac measures live on the **parameter space**;
the kernels generate a density on the **data space**.

# Dirac measure versus indicator function

These two expressions are related but have different types:

$$
\delta_a(A)=\mathbf 1_A(a).
$$

- $\delta_a$ takes a measurable set $A$ as input and returns its probability;
- $\mathbf 1_A$ takes a point $a$ as input and reports membership.

Confusing their inputs is a common source of notation errors.

# Common mistakes

1. **Calling a point mass an ordinary continuous density.**
   It has no density relative to Lebesgue measure.
2. **Writing $\delta_a(a)=1$ as the definition.**
   The measure is defined on sets: $\delta_a(A)=\mathbf 1(a\in A)$.
3. **Saying a DP mixture is discrete because its mixing distribution is
   discrete.**
   The induced sampling density may be continuous.
4. **Treating a Dirac measure as a small-variance normal distribution.**
   $N(a,\sigma^2)$ converges weakly to $\delta_a$ as $\sigma\downarrow0$, but
   no fixed positive $\sigma$ gives the same measure.

Here **weak convergence** means that

$$
\int h(x)N(a,\sigma^2)(dx)\longrightarrow h(a)
$$

for every bounded continuous $h$. This definition is sufficient for the
statement; the [consistency note](posterior-consistency.qmd#weak-neighborhoods)
compares weak convergence with stronger notions.

# Check your understanding

Select each **Answer** box after working out the question yourself.

**1. What is $\delta_a(A)$ when $a\notin A$?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

$\delta_a(A)=0$. A Dirac measure at $a$ assigns mass one to a set exactly when
that set contains $a$; otherwise it assigns mass zero.
:::

**2. Why does $\delta_a$ not have a Lebesgue density?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

The singleton $\{a\}$ has Lebesgue measure zero but
$\delta_a(\{a\})=1$. Therefore $\delta_a\not\ll\lambda$, so no
Radon--Nikodym derivative $d\delta_a/d\lambda$ exists. An ordinary function
integrated over a zero-length singleton could not produce mass one there.
:::

**3. Evaluate $\int x^2\delta_3(dx)$.**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

A Dirac measure evaluates the integrand at its atom:

$$
\int x^2\delta_3(dx)=3^2=9.
$$
:::

**4. Is $\sum_iW_i\delta_{X_i}$ a function, a probability measure, or both?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

When $W_i\geq0$ and $\sum_iW_i=1$, it is a probability measure. Like every
measure, it is technically a set function:

$$
A\longmapsto\sum_iW_i\mathbf 1(X_i\in A).
$$

It is **not** an ordinary pointwise density with respect to Lebesgue measure.
Calling it a function without naming its set-valued input can obscure that
distinction.
:::

**5. How can a discrete DP draw generate a continuous mixture density?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

If $G=\sum_jW_j\delta_{\Theta_j}$ is discrete on parameter space, then mixing
continuous kernels gives

$$
f_G(x)=\int k(x\mid\theta)G(d\theta)
=\sum_jW_jk(x\mid\Theta_j).
$$

The atoms choose kernel parameters; each kernel spreads mass over observation
space. Thus discreteness of $G$ does not imply discreteness of $f_G$.
:::
